newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-WTA TOUR UNIMPRESSED BY WIMBLEDON PRIZE MONEY.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-WTA TOUR UNIMPRESSED BY WIMBLEDON PRIZE MONEY.

text.p: The Women's Tennis Association expressed disappointment on Thursday at the Wimbledon committee's decision not to allocate equal prize money to men and women at this year's championships.

The men's singles champion will receive 415,000 pounds ($673,000), compared with the women's first prize of 373,500 pounds ($606,000), with Wimbledon chairman John Curry saying he saw "no good reason" to close the gap.
The WTA Tour's argument is that equal prizemoney should be paid from the quarter-finals onwards.
"There is a worldwide boom in women's tennis due to increased depth in fields and the rise of our young stars," said a Tour statement.

"In each of the last four years the women's final has been the most dramatic of all the matches during the fortnight, while in each of the last six years the women have consistently delivered more seeded players through to the quarter-finals."
The WTA are to continue to lobby the All England Club, but Curry insists the current pay structure is fair.
"We look at it very seriously every year but having considered all the facts we felt we had no good reason to change the way we are," said Curry.
"It's still the public's view that they prefer the men's matches to the women's."
Total prize money has increased by 6.5 percent to 6.88 million pounds ($11.2 million) and for the first time incorporates "per diem" payments to players in the qualifying tournament.
This year's Wimbledon, from June 23 to July 6, will also see the opening of the new number one court, which will extend the potential capacity of the grounds to 32,000.

Curry believes the considerable investment in rebuilding work will keep Wimbledon at the forefront of the game. "We constantly strive to ensure Wimbledon retains its premier position. We feel the prize money is a suitable reward for the endeavours of the players who are the best in the world."
